en: The Sūtra on the Three Turnings of the Previous Life, translated by the Śramaṇa Faju of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats.
All these great sages were the most venerable among them, for they all knew the thoughts in the minds of others, with the sole exception of Ānanda.
At that time, the Buddha emerged from the vihāra and sat in mid-air, surrounded by an assembly of countless hundreds of thousands of people whom he taught the Dharma;
there were also seventy thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom had attained various dhāraṇīs.
At that time, the Buddha’s facial complexion was more radiant than usual; light issued forth from his face and shone throughout all the worlds.
Then the Buddha smiled, and five-colored rays of light issued from his mouth, ascending as far as the Brahma Heaven.

When the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, bestow the prediction of enlightenment upon their disciples, light radiates forth to illuminate the Four Heavenly Kings; the light then returns to circle the Buddha three times and enters through the center of his soles.

When the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, bestow the prediction of the path of the Pratyekabuddha, light issues from their mouths, travels to illuminate the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and returns to circle the Buddha three times before entering through his navel.

When the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, bestow the prediction of the Buddha-way, light radiates forth to illuminate the Brahma-heaven and returns to encircle the Buddha three times before entering through the crown of his head.
At that time, the earth deities all simultaneously raise their voices, saying:
"In this way, the Buddha perceives three matters—whether past, future, or present—and proclaims various predictions."
The celestial deities of space, the Four Heavenly Kings, the gods from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven up to the Brahmā Heaven, all raised their voices and said:
"Thus he has spoken on these three matters and various resolutions concerning the past,
the future, and the present."
"Shall I bestow upon them the prediction of the stage of Disciple (śrāvaka-bhūmi), the prediction of the stage of Pratyekabuddha, or the prediction of the stage of Buddha?
At that time, the Brahmās all descended, and from there up to the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, they all descended.
At that time, there was an assembly of countless hundreds of thousands of people: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
The Venerable Ānanda then knew seven matters concerning the Dharma; what were these seven?
First, knowing the meaning;
second, understanding the Dharma;
third, comprehending the timing.
Fourth, discerning the joints;
fifth, clarifying the assembly;
sixth, knowing the affairs of the body.
Seventh, knowing the affairs of others.
The worthy Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and praised the Buddha in verse, saying:
"Having attained the pure eye of wisdom, clear and excellent, The Honored One’s faculties are tranquil and settled—this is the *pāramitā* of infinite peace."
His radiance shines afar with a golden hue; O Divine Illuminator, who can fulfill this wish?
Who now has resolved their mind upon the Buddha-way?
Who sits beneath the tree to subdue Māra?
Who now shall take up the benefit of the Buddha’s supreme path?
O Moon-faced One, pray tell us why you smile?
When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, smiles, light radiates from his face; his smile surpasses that of ordinary men.
"At this very moment, an assembly of hundreds of thousands of people has gathered; the Buddha shall now speak of it according to the circumstances.
Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"Venerable One, God among Gods!"
Those who possess lust, anger, and delusion laugh because of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena;
but the God among Gods has severed lust, anger, and delusion—for what reason does he laugh?
O God among Gods!
Was this not asked by Śāriputra?
Nor was it asked by Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, or Śāriputra-Bilika?
The Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, possess six unique qualities not shared [with others]. What are these six?
First, the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, possess the wisdom that knows the past without any obstruction.
Second, the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, possess the wisdom of the future that is unimpeded;
third, the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, also possess the wisdom of the present that is unimpeded;
fourth, the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, possess the wisdom of their physical conduct.
Fifth, the wisdom spoken from the mouths of the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods;
sixth, the wisdom of the mental intentions of the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods.
These are the six.
"The Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, have nothing they do not see or hear; the Buddhas preach the wisdom of the Buddha-way!
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In a past age, there was a land named Utpalavati. That land was wealthy, prosperous, and flourishing, with the five grains ripening in abundance; its people were peaceful and secure, and their numbers were beyond calculation."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"At that time, in the kingdom of Uppalavanna, there was a king named Pārasī who was preeminent among all the kingdoms."
In the governance he administered through his edicts and instructions, he ruled the kingdom with the True Dharma (*saddharma*), such that the use of the whip and staff was not employed.
At that time, the people lived for twenty thousand years.
Later, when that king passed away, there was in that country a courtesan of supreme beauty, whose countenance was upright and most exquisite.
That woman went to another's house, where the master of the house had given birth to a son; she then reached out her hand and pulled at the boy’s arm.
The courtesan asked him, "What do you intend to do by pulling at this child?"
He replied,
"I am hungry and wish to eat it. He asked:
"Is there no rice to eat?
He replied, "There is none."
The courtesan replied, "Wait a moment; I shall bring food for you.
He answered:
"Before you have even stepped out the door, I shall die of hunger; how could I possibly wait for you to bring me food?
The courtesan thought to herself, "If I take my son away, his mother will surely die of hunger."
"If I leave him behind, he will surely seize and devour my child.
What should I do to ensure that both mother and child find peace and security?
The courtesan immediately took a sharp knife, cut off her own two breasts, and gave them to him; the mother then ate them.
The lustful woman asked,
"Have you finished eating?
He replied:
"I am already satiated.
The courtesan’s two breasts bled profusely, and she returned to her home.
At that time, a man arrived at the courtesan's house, desiring to engage in unrighteous acts with her; upon seeing her, he spoke:
"Who took this woman of such exquisite beauty and cut her breasts like this?
Thinking thus, he felt compassion and attended to her with the affection of a brother and sister, no longer giving rise to thoughts of desire.
The man then asked, "Sister!
Who has taken you as his wife in this manner?"
He replied: "There is no one who has disturbed me.
I went to another's house, and just as the master was about to give birth, he immediately pulled his child away."
I asked him,
"What do you wish to do?
He replied to me:
"I am hungry and wish to take my son's flesh and eat it.
I asked, "Do you have no food to eat?"
He replied to me, saying, "There is none. I said:
"Wait a moment; I must go fetch rice for you.
He replied to me, saying, "Before you have even stepped out the door, I shall die of hunger."
I thought to myself:
"If I take this child away, the mother will surely die;
yet if I abandon him here, she will surely seize and devour him."
"I then cut off my breasts and gave them to him to eat.
When the man heard these words, he immediately fell to the ground and lost consciousness.
The courtesan then took water and sprinkled it over him; after a long time, he finally regained his breath.
The man asked, "Sister,
will you manifest your utmost sincerity for my sake?
The courtesan replied:
"Yes," the man said,
"I have never before encountered such a difficulty."
"If what you say is truly sincere and not false, then your sister's breasts shall return to their former state.
At that very moment, the woman's breasts returned to their former state, and there was no scar remaining.
Śakra Devānām Indra, seeing the lustful woman with his divine eye, said:
"This woman of supreme beauty has performed such meritorious acts through giving; I fear she will come and seize my seat."

He then transformed himself into a brahmin, holding a branch of jewels and a jar of cleansing powder, and carrying a golden mendicant’s staff; he went to beg for alms at the house of this courtesan and said, "Give me a portion of your alms."
The woman then took a golden bowl, filled it with rice, and went out to give it to the brahmin; however, the brahmin immediately stepped back and refused to accept it.
The woman of superior beauty asked the practitioner, "Why do you step back and refuse to accept the food?"
He replied, "I do not need food.
I have heard that you are giving away milk; is this indeed true?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The brahmin then questioned him with a verse, saying:
"What vow do you seek?
How could Śakra be a Brahmā?
Is it for the sake of seeking the King of Many Treasures? Such a vow is difficult indeed."
The woman of exquisite beauty replied in verse,
saying: “The Brahmin who is unconditioned, Free from birth, old age, sickness, and death,
In the sorrowless and pure state— O Brahmin, it is him that I seek.”
The brahmin said: "I ask you:
when you gave milk as an act of almsgiving, did your mind undergo any change?"
The woman replied,
"Brahmin! I shall manifest my utmost sincerity for you."
He replied, "Show it to me.
The woman said:
"If my sincerity in holding this milk as an act of giving is unswerving, may I transform this female body and become a man.
As soon as these words were finished, she was immediately transformed into a man.
At that time, after King Uparava had ruled the kingdom for five thousand years, he passed away.
His ministers and attendants, having heard that the lustful woman had been transformed into a man, thought to themselves:
"We shall indeed establish this person as king; as a ruler, he shall govern the kingdom with the True Dharma."
They then established him together as king.

He did not employ whips or staves, but ruled the country with the True Dharma (*saddharma*). He delighted in giving away gold, silver, and precious jewels at the four city gates and throughout the streets and alleys. To those who desired food, drink, clothing, incense, flowers, rooms, seats, houses, gold, silver, precious jewels, moon-bright pearls, jade, lapis lazuli, crystal, coral, or agate, he gave them according to their wishes.

He taught all the people under heaven to observe the eightfold precepts of the fast. Thus he governed the kingdom for five hundred years; there was no need for plowing or sowing, as rice grew naturally, pure, fragrant, and exquisite. It was free from coarseness; what was harvested today would sprout again by dawn, and as soon as the grain was taken, its stalks would sink away and disappear.

They partake of the flavor of shared food; after consuming all such flavorful food, their teeth do not fall out, nor do they grow old, nor do they fall ill, nor do they become hunched. Their complexions remain unchanged, and their stature is perfectly uniform.
Their physical endowments are likewise equal, just like those in the continent of Uttarakuru.
The king thought to himself:
"What is so strange about my giving to human beings?
It is only when I give to birds and beasts that it becomes difficult."
At that time, King Sūgandha anointed his body with perfumes and entered a secluded place in the mountains, where he lay upon a rock.

All manner of birds came and began to devour his flesh until he passed away and was reborn into a brahmin family—one of great wealth, possessing immeasurable gold, silver, and precious jewels. When ten months had passed, he was born, and his appearance was peerlessly handsome and upright.
As soon as he was born, four handmaidens together nurtured him:
the first mistress attended to wiping his body;
the second mistress attended to bathing him.
The third mistress nursed him;
the fourth mistress carried him.
As the child grew up, the four women attended to him together, deliberating that no one else should see him, while five hundred court ladies served them to provide mutual entertainment.
He then secretly went out toward the marketplace, where he observed those engaged in trade and the poor who were begging; filled with a sense of compassion, he said:
"If these people were wealthy and happy, they would no longer engage in such trade and peddling."
At that time, he spoke these verses himself:
"What is this state of my body and mind?
It is exceedingly firm and remains unbroken. While I abide in a state of sovereign peace and bliss, I behold all the people who suffer in toil."
He hurried back and said to his parents,
"I wish to shave off my hair and beard and go into the empty mountains to dwell beneath a tree.
His parents would not permit it.
Why is this? You have but one son, whom you love most dearly:
"I prayed to the mountains, rivers, sun, moon, and various devas, and only then did I obtain this one son."
"If I do not see you, I shall die of grief.
Refusing to let him go, the son lay prostrate on the ground; for one day, two days, up to five days, he neither ate nor drank.

When his close relatives and friends heard that this boy wished to leave home to study the Way and shave his hair and beard, but his parents would not permit it, he lay prostrate on the bare ground for five days, refusing food and drink.
All his close relatives and friends went together to where he was and exhorted him, saying:
"Young man!
Why do you not rise to bathe, eat, and adorn yourself, but instead shave off your hair and beard to dwell among the trees, delighting in the Way?"
The youth also did not respond;
he spoke thus for three days.
Then his relatives and close friends went together to his parents' place and said:
"Listen, let him go to study the Way; if he finds it pleasing, he may come and go to see us as often as he likes, but if he does not find it pleasing, he shall return home.
His parents replied, "Yes!"

Having seen that they had granted permission, the son then personally tended to them for six or seven days; he circumambulated his parents three times, paid them homage, and then entered a secluded place to sit and practice the Way. Afterward, he went to another large grove of trees.

"There were two practitioners of the Way sitting there who had attained the five supernatural powers; through their sincerity they sought the Way and remained free from lustful desire. The youth then went to where they were and asked: 'What is being done here?'"
He replied, "I am sitting here in the open air practicing dhyāna and contemplating the Way; for the sake of the people, I am performing these arduous ascetic practices.
The youth said:
"I, too, shall sit in meditation in the open air for the sake of the people, contemplating the Way.
The two practitioners said,
"Excellent!"
The youth then sat in meditation beneath a great grove of trees.
For the sake of the people therein, he practiced the Way with diligent austerity and immediately attained the five supernormal powers;
his vigor surpassed that of the two practitioners of the Way, for he was a Great Sage of supreme honor.
In the midst of those trees was a tigress pregnant with young.
According to the custom of the practitioners, they would only eat fruit that fell naturally from the tree and would not pluck it from the branches.

While several practitioners were traveling together in search of fruits and melons, they encountered a pregnant tigress. One young practitioner said to the other two practitioners, "This tigress will soon give birth;
having been hungry for many days, I fear she will devour her own cubs."
"Who is able to take this body and eat it?
Maitreya Bodhisattva replied,
"I shall take this body and eat it."
After gathering fruits and returning, he saw that the tigress was starving from lack of milk and intended to devour her own cubs. The practitioner said to the two other practitioners:
"The tigress is already starving from lack of milk and intends to eat her own cubs."
"Who can take this body and eat it?
They then went together to where the starving tigress was. As the tigress opened her eyes and gaped her mouth toward them, the two practitioners were both struck with fear and flew up into the void.
One of them said:
"O practitioner!
Such is your utmost sincerity."
Previously you said,
"I shall offer my body as food for the starving tigress.
Why is it that now you have flown up into the void?
One of the practitioners was moved by compassion and tears fell from his eyes; looking around him, he saw nothing else.

The young practitioner took a sharp blade and pierced his right arm until blood flowed; he pierced himself in this manner at seven places, letting the blood enter the tiger’s mouth so that it might drink it. He then threw himself before the starving tiger to be eaten, and died.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you wish to know who that woman of exquisite beauty was at that time?
It was indeed my own self."
The one who was established as king at that time was also my own self;
the son of a brahmin who threw himself to feed a starving tiger was also my own self;
and the two practitioners were Kāśyapa and Maitreya Bodhisattva.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Because I practiced the path with diligent exertion, I have transcended nine kalpas and emerged before Maitreya.
It is thus, Ānanda!”

Having diligently practiced the Way for sixty kalpas, by giving away his hands, feet, nose, ears, head, eyes, flesh, and muscles, as well as his wife, sons, daughters, and fine garments and food, he subdued sixty billion Māras, and thirty-four billion attained the Buddha-way.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“If all people were to know the merit of giving as I know it, then even one who is destitute and seeking a livelihood, having obtained a single meal to sustain their life—
should they not eat it and instead die— they would rather not eat it themselves and give it to a virtuous person to receive.”
Ānanda! I recall the gifts I gave in past lives; because of this, my facial complexion is bright and radiant, and the light of my smile issues from my mouth, pervading the entire trichiliocosm.

When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, four thousand two hundred bhikṣus attained liberation through the mind of no-remainder; eighty nayutas of devas and humans gave rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment; and seventy thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena.

When the Buddha had spoken thus, the venerable Ānanda, along with the entire assembly—including the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and the people of the world—were all filled with joy; they came forward, prostrated before the Buddha, and departed.
The Sūtra on the Three Turnings of the Previous Life.
